node.name: Random variables and distributions
node.description: Map outcomes to numerical values and describe their mass or cumulative distribution.
node.details:
A random variable assigns a number to each outcome of a random experiment, such as the number of heads in three coin flips, which can be 0, 1, 2, or 3. For a discrete random variable, the probability mass function lists P(X = x) for each possible value; for three fair flips these are 1/8, 3/8, 3/8, and 1/8, which must sum to 1.

The cumulative distribution function F(x) = P(X ≤ x) accumulates those probabilities, so here F(1) = 1/8 + 3/8 = 1/2. Distributions let you answer questions about ranges of values, and they are the basis for expected value, variance, and named models such as the binomial, geometric, and Poisson distributions. Continuous random variables, such as a measured length, need densities instead of probabilities for individual values.

node.name: Wave speed, frequency, and wavelength
node.description: Use v = fλ to link how fast a wave travels, how often it oscillates, and the spacing of its crests.
node.details:
A wave is a disturbance that travels, while each bit of the medium only oscillates about its resting position. Frequency f is the number of oscillations per second (hertz), period T = 1/f is the time for one oscillation, and wavelength λ is the distance between neighbouring crests. Because a wave advances one wavelength per period, its speed is v = fλ.

Sound in air at about 20 °C travels near 343 m/s, so a 1000 Hz tone has λ = 343/1000 ≈ 0.34 m. The frequency is set by the source; when a wave passes into a new medium its speed and wavelength change, but its frequency stays the same. Ultrasonic ranging is a practical use: a sensor times an echo, and because the pulse travels out and back, the distance is d = vt/2. An echo returning after 5.8 ms means about 343 × 0.0058 / 2 ≈ 1.0 m.

node.name: Sampling and bias
node.description: Distinguish a population from an observed sample and identify selection or measurement bias.
node.details:
A population is the entire group you want to learn about; a sample is the part you actually observe. Statistics computed from a sample estimate population values, and an estimate is only as good as the way the sample was collected. Random sampling, where every member has a known chance of selection, protects against systematic distortion and allows the remaining uncertainty to be quantified.

Bias is a consistent error in one direction that does not shrink with more data. Selection bias arises when some groups are more likely to be included, such as surveying only people at home on weekday afternoons. Measurement bias comes from faulty instruments or leading questions, and nonresponse bias appears when those who decline differ from those who answer. Random sampling error, by contrast, varies from sample to sample and decreases as the sample grows, which is why a huge biased sample can be less accurate than a small random one.

node.name: Sampling and aliasing
node.description: Understand how taking discrete samples of a continuous signal can make fast signals masquerade as slow ones.
node.details:
A digital system never sees a signal continuously; it records values at regular instants, at a sampling rate fs. The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem says a signal can be captured unambiguously only if all of its frequency content lies below fs/2, the Nyquist frequency. Anything above that limit folds back and appears as a lower frequency, called an alias.

Example: sampled at 1000 Hz, a 900 Hz cosine produces exactly the same sample values as a 100 Hz cosine, because |900 − 1000| = 100. Once sampled, nothing in the data tells the two apart. The film effect of wagon wheels seeming to spin backward is the same phenomenon. In robotics this matters for motor current, vibration, and control loops: an unexpected slow oscillation in logged data may really be a fast disturbance aliased down. Sampling fast enough and filtering before sampling are the standard defences.

node.name: Complex-number arithmetic
node.description: Extend real arithmetic with an imaginary unit whose square is minus one and use conjugates for division.
node.details:
Complex numbers extend the reals by adding the imaginary unit i, defined by i² = −1. Every complex number can be written a + bi, with real part a and imaginary part b, which lets equations like x² + 4 = 0 have solutions, x = 2i and x = −2i. Addition and subtraction work part by part: (3 + 2i) + (1 − 4i) = 4 − 2i. Multiplication uses distribution and then replaces i² with −1: (3 + 2i)(1 − 4i) = 3 − 12i + 2i − 8i² = 11 − 10i.

Division relies on the conjugate. The conjugate of a + bi is a − bi, and their product a² + b² is real. To divide, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator: (5 + 5i)/(1 + 2i) becomes (15 − 5i)/5 = 3 − i. Powers of i repeat in a cycle of four, i, −1, −i, 1, so i¹⁰ = i² = −1.

node.name: Definite integrals and accumulation
node.description: Interpret a definite integral as signed accumulation, built as the limit of increasingly fine Riemann sums.
node.details:
The definite integral ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx measures the signed accumulation of f over the interval [a, b]. To build it, slice the interval into n strips of width Δx, multiply a sample height from each strip by Δx, and add; this Riemann sum approaches the integral as the strips get thinner. With f(x) = x² on [0, 2] and four strips, the left sum is 0.5(0 + 0.25 + 1 + 2.25) = 1.75, while the exact value is 8/3 ≈ 2.67. Left, right, midpoint, and trapezoidal sums differ only in how each strip's height is chosen.

Signed means area below the x-axis counts as negative, so ∫ from 0 to 2π of sin x dx equals 0 even though the curve encloses area; to get total geometric area, split at the crossings and add absolute values. Integrals turn rates into totals: integrating velocity gives displacement, and integrating a density gives total mass. Linearity and symmetry simplify many calculations.

node.name: Regression and residual analysis
node.description: Fit a relationship and inspect residual patterns rather than relying only on a fitted line.
node.details:
Regression fits a model that predicts a response variable from one or more explanatory variables. In simple linear regression, the least-squares line ŷ = a + bx is the line that minimises the sum of squared residuals, where each residual is an observed value minus its predicted value, e = y − ŷ.

Residual analysis checks whether the model suits the data. Plot residuals against x or against the fitted values: a good fit leaves a patternless band centred on zero. A curved pattern suggests a nonlinear relationship, a funnel shape means the scatter changes with x, and isolated large residuals point to outliers or influential points. If a straight line is fitted to data that really follow y = x² over a range of positive x, the residuals are positive at both ends and negative in the middle. A high r² alone does not guarantee a suitable model, so inspect residuals before trusting a calibration or prediction.

node.name: Antiderivatives
node.description: Recover a family of functions from its derivative and use an initial condition to fix the integration constant.
node.details:
An antiderivative of f is any function F whose derivative is f. Because constants differentiate to zero, antiderivatives come as a family F(x) + C, written as the indefinite integral ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C. Basic results come from reading derivative rules backwards: ∫ xⁿ dx = x^(n+1)/(n + 1) + C for n ≠ −1, ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + C, ∫ e^x dx = e^x + C, and ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C. Sums and constant multiples are handled term by term, and any answer can be checked by differentiating it.

An initial condition selects one member of the family. If an object's acceleration is a(t) = −9.8 m/s² and its velocity at t = 0 is 5 m/s, then v(t) = −9.8t + C, and v(0) = 5 forces C = 5. Integrating again with a known starting position gives the position function. Antiderivatives are also the working tool for evaluating definite integrals through the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

specification.source_explanation_unreviewed:
An antiderivative of f is any function F whose derivative is f. Because constants differentiate to zero, antiderivatives come as a family F(x) + C, written as the indefinite integral ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C. Basic results come from reading derivative rules backwards: ∫ xⁿ dx = x^(n+1)/(n + 1) + C for n ≠ −1, ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + C, ∫ e^x dx = e^x + C, and ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C. Sums and constant multiples are handled term by term, and any answer can be checked by differentiating it.

An initial condition selects one member of the family. If an object's acceleration is a(t) = −9.8 m/s² and its velocity at t = 0 is 5 m/s, then v(t) = −9.8t + C, and v(0) = 5 forces C = 5. Integrating again with a known starting position gives the position function. Antiderivatives are also the working tool for evaluating definite integrals through the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

node.name: Fundamental theorem of calculus
node.description: Connect accumulation with differentiation and evaluate definite integrals as F(b) − F(a) using antiderivatives.
node.details:
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus shows that integration and differentiation undo each other. The first part says that if f is continuous and A(x) = ∫ from a to x of f(t) dt is the area accumulated up to x, then A'(x) = f(x): area accumulates at a rate equal to the curve's height. The second part says that if F is any antiderivative of f on [a, b], then ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a).

The second part replaces limits of Riemann sums with quick calculations: ∫ from 0 to 2 of x² dx = 8/3 − 0 = 8/3, and ∫ from 0 to π of sin x dx = −cos π + cos 0 = 2. The continuity condition matters. Applying the formula blindly to 1/x² on [−1, 1] gives −2, which is impossible for a positive function, because 1/x² is undefined at 0; that integral is improper and actually diverges. In applied terms, total change equals the integral of the rate of change.

node.name: Improper integrals
node.description: Evaluate integrals over unbounded intervals or with unbounded integrands by taking limits.
node.details:
An improper integral is a definite integral whose interval is infinite or whose integrand blows up somewhere on the interval. The fix is to replace the troublesome bound with a variable and take a limit. For example, ∫ from 1 to ∞ of 1/x² dx is the limit as b → ∞ of (1 − 1/b), which is 1, so the integral converges. By contrast, ∫ from 1 to ∞ of 1/x dx grows like ln b and diverges. In general, ∫ from 1 to ∞ of 1/x^p dx converges only when p > 1.

Integrals of the second kind have a vertical asymptote: ∫ from 0 to 1 of 1/√x dx is the limit of 2 − 2√a as a → 0⁺, which is 2. An integral over the whole real line must be split at some point, and each piece must converge on its own; using arctangent, ∫ of 1/(1 + x²) from −∞ to ∞ equals π. Improper integrals appear in probability distributions, Laplace transforms, and the integral test for series.

node.name: Analog-to-digital conversion
node.description: Map an analog input range to discrete output codes and distinguish a converter's resolution from its accuracy.
node.details:
An analog-to-digital converter samples a voltage and reports it as an integer code. An N-bit converter has 2^N codes spread across its reference voltage, so one step, the least significant bit, is about Vref/2^N. A 12-bit converter with a 3.3 V reference has 4096 codes and a step of about 0.806 mV, so 1.65 V reads near code 2048. Even an ideal converter rounds, leaving up to ±½ LSB of quantisation error.

Resolution is the step size; accuracy is how close the reading is to the truth, and extra bits do not improve it. A reference that is 1% off gives 1% error however many bits there are, and offset, gain error, nonlinearity, noise, and incomplete settling of the sampling capacitor from a high-impedance source all add more. Sampling rate matters too: content above half the sample rate aliases to false lower frequencies, which is why an anti-alias filter is used. Keep inputs within the allowed range.

node.name: Laplace transforms
node.description: Transform time functions and derivative equations into a complex-frequency representation.
node.details:
The Laplace transform converts a function of time f(t), defined for t ≥ 0, into a function of a complex variable s through the improper integral F(s) = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(−st)·f(t) dt, which converges when the real part of s is large enough. Standard pairs include 1 → 1/s, e^(at) → 1/(s − a), and sin(ωt) → ω/(s² + ω²).

Its main use is the derivative rule L{y'} = s·Y(s) − y(0), with L{y''} = s²·Y(s) − s·y(0) − y'(0). Differentiation becomes multiplication by s and initial conditions enter automatically, so a linear ODE with constant coefficients turns into algebra. For y' + 2y = 1 with y(0) = 0, transforming gives s·Y + 2Y = 1/s, so Y(s) = 1/(s(s + 2)). Turning that back into a time function is the job of inverse Laplace methods. In control engineering, the ratio of the output transform to the input transform, with zero initial conditions, is called the transfer function.

node.name: Sensor calibration curves
node.description: Relate raw sensor readings to reference quantities and inspect offset, gain, nonlinearity, and residuals.
node.details:
A sensor reports a raw number, such as ADC counts or millivolts, that must be mapped to a physical quantity. A calibration curve is built by recording readings at several known reference values and fitting a model to them. The simplest is linear: quantity = gain × reading + offset. If a pressure sensor reads 410 counts at 0 kPa and 3690 counts at 200 kPa, the gain is 200 / 3280 ≈ 0.061 kPa per count and the offset is about −25 kPa.

After fitting, inspect the residuals, the differences between reference values and model predictions. Random scatter suggests the model is adequate; a curved pattern reveals nonlinearity that may need a polynomial or lookup table. A calibration holds only for the range and conditions used. Extrapolating beyond the tested points, or applying it at a different temperature or supply voltage, can produce errors the fit never saw, so record those conditions and the reference uncertainty.

node.name: Inertial measurement units
node.description: Distinguish accelerometer and gyroscope outputs, their biases, and the reference frames they are expressed in.
node.details:
An inertial measurement unit combines accelerometers and gyroscopes, often three of each on perpendicular axes, and sometimes a magnetometer. A gyroscope measures angular rate, in degrees or radians per second, about each axis of the sensor's own body frame. An accelerometer measures specific force, which is acceleration relative to free fall. That is why a board lying still on a table reads about 1 g upward rather than zero, while a board in free fall reads nearly zero.

This causes common misunderstandings. The accelerometer alone cannot separate gravity from motion, so tilt estimates are corrupted while the robot accelerates. Integrating gyroscope rate gives orientation, but any small bias accumulates into steadily growing drift, and double-integrating acceleration to get position drifts far faster. Readings are also in the sensor's frame and must be rotated into the robot or world frame. Calibration removes offsets and scale errors, and fusion filters combine the gyroscope's short-term accuracy with the accelerometer's long-term gravity reference.
